title: Africa Miss Universe beauty queens in limbo as US visa restrictions bite
description: Miss Universe Zimbabwe Roseanna Hall and several other contestants from Africa could miss this year's competition in Puerto Rico as they race to secur
body: Miss Universe Zimbabwe Roseanna Hall and several other contestants from Africa could miss this year's competition in Puerto Rico as they race to secure a US visa.Hall is due to represent Zimbabwe at the 75th edition of the Miss Universe pageant, with the winner set to be crowned on 24 November. But she has yet to obtain a visa to travel to the US territory."We have been back and forth, trying to get my visa approved," Hall said in a video posted on her Instagram page.Hall is not the only African contestant to be affected by the restrictions. Zambia has withdrawn its representative, Pamela Mubanga, from the competition because of US travel restrictions.Contestants began arriving in Puerto Rico on 8 November for registration, fittings and other pre-pageant activities, putting pressure on Hall, and others including the representative from South Sudan, to secure their visas. "Officially, today is the day I was supposed to be leaving for Puerto Rico for the 75th edition of Miss Universe," Hall said.Zimbabwe is among 19 countries subject to partial US travel restrictions introduced under the Presidential Proclamation 10998, which took effect on 1 January 2026. The measures suspend the issuance of visitor, student and exchange visas, as well as immigrant visas, to nationals of the affected countries. They also impose restrictions on other categories of non-immigrant visas.In a statement, the Miss Universe organization in Zambia said Mubanga's situation was a consequence of the travel restrictions rather than individual circumstances."Unlike situations where a contestant's visa is denied due to personal circumstances, documentation or organisational challenges, Mubanga's situation is linked to the United States' presidential travel restriction affecting Zambia and other African countries," the statement read.Mubanga, 25, a registered nurse, was crowned Miss Universe Zambia on 8 October and was due to represent the country at the international pageant.The statement said five other African countries faced similar difficulties, although it did not name them. Hall said she shared their concerns, adding that she had spent the past few weeks in South Africa trying to secure her visa."I am not alone in this predicament. Some of my African sisters are facing the same predicament, and I know exactly what they are going through," she said.Miss Universe South Sudan also expressed uncertainty about her participation, commenting on Hall's video: "It is 50/50 whether we will make it, Miss Universe."In another video posted three days earlier, Hall said she was still hoping to make it to Puerto Rico. She captioned the video: "The fight to get Zimbabwe to Puerto Rico continues,"The pageant's final is scheduled to take place at the José Miguel Agrelot Coliseum in San Juan.

schema.headline: Africa Miss Universe beauty queens in limbo as US visa restrictions bite

title: Aide to pro-Kremlin Ukrainian ex-PM badly hurt in Moscow car bomb
description: A car bomb attack in Moscow has wounded a former adviser to Ukrainian ex-prime minister Mykola Azarov, Russia's Investigative Committee says.Sergei Za
body: A car bomb attack in Moscow has wounded a former adviser to Ukrainian ex-prime minister Mykola Azarov, Russia's Investigative Committee says.Sergei Zavorotny, now a journalist and commentator, was behind the wheel of his black Toyota when the explosion happened and Azarov told Russian TV his condition in hospital was "rather critical".The car bomb went off a day after a Russian colonel was killed in another explosion in St Petersburg, and both blasts are seen as part of a series of attacks on military  and prominent figures linked to Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.Zavorotny, 72, worked as a press aide to Mykola Azarov in Kyiv until 2014.But when pro-Kremlin Ukrainian president Viktor Yanukovych was toppled from power, Azarov fled Kyiv for Russia and tried unsuccessfully to set up a government in exile.In a 2020 US Senate report on interference in the 2016 American presidential election, Zavorotny is described at the time as an SVR [Russian foreign intelligence] officer involved in influence operations. Russia's Investigative Committee said on Telegram on Friday: "Serhiy Zavorotny, a former adviser to the former Ukrainian Prime Minister Mykola Azarov, was injured while driving a car. He was taken to one of the city hospitals, where he is receiving medical care."It added: "A set of necessary investigative actions is being carried out. A number of examinations will be appointed, including medical and explosives."According to several unconfirmed reports, Zavorotny suffered a number of serious injuries after an explosive device was detonated remotely.Russia said the car bombs are the latest in a series of attacks targeting pro-Kremlin figures.On Thursday a car bomb in the Pushkinsky District of St Petersburg killed a member of the Russian military, again after it was attached to the base of the car and detonated remotely.The man targeted in the attack is yet to be named officially, but reputable sources suggest he was a high-ranking figure in the 6th Guards Air and Air Defence Forces Army.Overnight into Friday, Ukraine and Russia exchanged attacks on each other's territories.Ukrainian authorities said a hospital had been targeted by Russian bombardment.They added that three people, including a 17-year-old boy, were also killed in attacks across southern Odesa and Zaporizhzhia.Russia said a Ukrainian strike on an industrial facility in the central Samara region killed four people.And in the southern Volgograd region another four died after an industrial zone was hit by drones. A further person died in the Bryansk border region, an area that is often fired upon.Ukraine said these were retaliatory attacks in response to Russia's persistent targeting of its cities.

schema.headline: Aide to pro-Kremlin Ukrainian ex-PM badly hurt in Moscow car bomb

title: University of Nigeria Nsukka: Four Nigerian students die after sign-out party
description: Four Nigerian students have died after attending a party in the south-eastern town of Nsukka to celebrate the end of their final exams.The cause of de
body: Four Nigerian students have died after attending a party in the south-eastern town of Nsukka to celebrate the end of their final exams.The cause of death has not been confirmed but police spokesman Daniel Ndukwe said the two men and two women had reportedly fallen ill after consuming alcoholic drinks at the party.The University of Nigeria Nsukka has declared three days of mourning, during which academic and social activities will be suspended.The tragedy comes amid a wider crackdown on fake and adulterated alcoholic drinks in Nigeria, where the food and drug regulator has been raiding suspected producers of unsafe food and beverages.The university's Vice-Chancellor, Professor Simon Ortuanya, said the university had received a distress call at 22:00 on Wednesday, and sent security personnel to a house party at Praise Lodge, outside the campus in Nsukka's Hilltop area."The preliminary investigation and interim report point to alleged alcohol abuse or drug paraphernalia and things like that. But we are not conclusive on those matters," he said.He described the deaths as "tragic and painful"."As a community, we mourn, not just alone, we mourn with the families, the parents that have suffered these years to train the men and women in their studies," he said.Ortuanya also announced a ban on signing-out celebrations, which are commonly held by final-year students to mark the completion of their studies.The celebrations often involve parties, dancing, photographs and friends signing one another's shirts. He urged students to use graduation as a time to reflect on their university experience and prepare for life beyond campus.The university said it was working with security agencies to establish what had caused the deaths.The police have also launched an investigation. They said alcoholic drinks had been recovered from the scene and the bodies taken to a mortuary for autopsies.The investigation comes amid wider concerns about unsafe alcoholic drinks in Nigeria.In September, dozens of people fell ill after consuming locally made alcoholic drinks and herbal mixtures in communities across Ondo State, south-west Nigeria.More than 11 people died in the Araromi-Obu area, while more than 50 others were hospitalised.Investigations found that some of the drinks had been contaminated with methanol, a highly toxic form of alcohol that can cause blindness and death.Nigeria's food and drug regulator, Nafdac, reported more than 150 cases, including 48 confirmed deaths. More than 80 people were hospitalised, and five lost their sight.The regulator has been carrying out raids across the country, targeting facilities suspected of producing fake or adulterated alcoholic drinks, food and beverages.Nigeria has long struggled with the sale of unsafe and adulterated products, which campaigners warn pose a serious threat to public health.

schema.headline: University of Nigeria Nsukka: Four Nigerian students die after sign-out party

title: Rosenberg: Uncompromising Putin ups demands for peace with Ukraine
description: Russia's President Vladimir Putin says he wishes "eternal peace" for Ukraine.That is the same Russian president who ordered the full-scale invasion of
body: Russia's President Vladimir Putin says he wishes "eternal peace" for Ukraine.That is the same Russian president who ordered the full-scale invasion of Russia's neighbour nearly five years ago and who continues to reject the idea of a comprehensive ceasefire.And what, in Moscow's view, is a prerequisite for peace?The Kremlin spelt it out after talks with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner: "A new, long-term architecture of indivisible security and peace."Translated from Kremlin-speak, it means Moscow wants to change the security set-up of Europe in a way that benefits Russia.What Russia is pushing for is, potentially, the biggest change to European security arrangements since the end of the Cold War.The Kremlin has put back on the table its controversial proposal from December 2021 – the "draft treaties" with the US and Nato which would not only have put the brakes on the alliance's eastward enlargement by giving Moscow cast-iron guarantees that, for instance, Ukraine and Georgia would never be allowed to join, but also rolled back Nato military infrastructure from countries of central and eastern Europe which became Nato members following the dissolution of the Soviet Union.Western leaders dismissed such demands as an unacceptable Russian ultimatum. Two months later Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.The "draft treaties" were put away. Now they are out of the geopolitical filing cabinet, and being quoted again by the Kremlin.What is more, Yuri Ushakov, Putin's foreign policy aide, has suggested that Moscow is about to "add certain new considerations" to its list of demands in light of Western efforts "to inflict a strategic defeat on Russia".That does not mean, of course, that Western governments will accept them.But the fact that the question of European security is featuring now in discussions on Ukraine is viewed here as a victory for Moscow."In December 2021 Russia actively proposed that Nato rethink the security system in Europe," wrote newspaper Komsomolskaya Pravda earlier this week."Our proposals were almost laughed at."Having secured one victory by forcing the West to think about security, our diplomats need a second by making the West heed Russia's concerns about Nato enlargement."The EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, has called Russia's demands for a new European security architecture a "trap" designed to "shift attention away from a ceasefire"."The sequencing of Ukraine-Russia talks is important," Kallas wrote on social media. "The priority should be securing a ceasefire, followed by a peace agreement. Only then can there be discussions on Europe's wider security architecture."Europe's problem is that, right now, it is not at the table.Moscow has had no desire to give it a chair. It has slammed European leaders for their military support for Kyiv and tough stance on Russia.This week's peace talks in Abu Dhabi involved Ukraine, Russia and the US.After his discussions in Moscow, Witkoff indicated that Putin had agreed to the idea of European representatives joining the next round of Ukraine peace talks.But on Friday the Kremlin indicated a final decision on European participation had not been taken."Once we understand their true intentions and their readiness to facilitate the peace process, then it will be possible to take a decision about dialogue on Ukraine in a wider format," said Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov.And what of Putin?At the talks with Witkoff and Kushner he was sounding uncompromising and confident.You can see why.The Americans are knocking at his door and seeking a deal and the Europeans are contemplating contacts with him. Last month the leaders of Norway and Finland reached out and called him.And next week in Shenzhen, China, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation summit, Putin may have a separate meeting with Donald Trump and Xi Jinping. Russian media are already comparing them to the "Big Three" - Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill - who met in 1945 to reorganise post-World War Two Europe.And yet, after nearly five years of war, Russia has suffered huge losses on the battlefield.The Russian economy is under increasing pressure.Ukrainian drone strikes continue to target Russian oil refineries, sparking fears of new fuel shortages.But, so far, none of this has convinced the Kremlin leader to end the fighting.

schema.headline: Rosenberg: Uncompromising Putin ups demands for peace with Ukraine

title: Microsoft 'deeply sorry' for global outage after almost 24 hours of disruption
description: Microsoft has said it is "deeply sorry" for the service outage to its products, including Outlook and Teams, which has caused disruption around the wo
body: Microsoft has said it is "deeply sorry" for the service outage to its products, including Outlook and Teams, which has caused disruption around the world.Services were broadly recovering by Friday afternoon, nearly 24 hours after issues began. Microsoft said it was making "encouraging progress", but added it does not know when services will fully recover.The outage hit more than 70 countries, disrupting everything from business operations to government services and personal users. More than 430 million people use the affected products worldwide.Microsoft said it was a technical issue introduced during a "network capacity upgrade" and not related to cyber or artificial intelligence agents.Experts said the event was a "stark reminder" of how heavily businesses and vital services rely on a small group of big tech providers.Users began reporting they were having trouble accessing Microsoft 365 products on Thursday.By Friday, the far-reaching issue was affecting institutions from the Japanese government and the Philippines Supreme Court to the Australian spy agency, and trains, hospitals and courts in North America.In the UK, some parts of the NHS, including GPs and hospitals, were affected, as were some schools and police forces.UK cyber minister Liz Lloyd said the incident had "limited" impact on critical frontline services such as 999 calls, and there had been no disruption to the transport network.In Canada, however, the national rail network said passengers may not be able to receive email updates about their trips, and hospitals across the country also had issues with emails.In the US, staff members from the House of Representatives told Politico it had set back an entire day of legislative work as everything was on Microsoft's Outlook.Singapore's government acknowledged some of its systems had been impacted, and in India, the outage disrupted work for many on Friday.In Turkey, advisers and officials attending the COP31 climate summit in Antalya were left frustrated by being unable to access Outlook.The issues also affected smaller businesses and individuals.Microsoft first acknowledged users in the Americas were unable to access Exchange Online mailboxes at 17:54 GMT on Thursday, and shortly after warned the disruption was possibly affecting Microsoft 365 globally.While it launched an investigation and engineers began working to restore services, by 04:36 on Friday Microsoft was reporting only a "partial recovery" in some parts of the world.By 13:32, the tech giant said there were "broader improvements" in North America, "sustained improvements" across much of Europe and "encouraging recovery signals" in the Asia Pacific region.Microsoft said it restored services gradually due to the scale of the problem and to help ensure services remain stable once they are up and running again."We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners," a Microsoft spokesperson said."We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously."Microsoft said it has no "ETA" for when services will be fully recovered.A full post-incident report will be released once Microsoft has completed a review.Experts said while workers may have been happy to not have email access for the day, the incident showed the dependence many organisations have on these cloud-based services."The global Microsoft outage is a stark reminder of how heavily we rely on a handful of big tech providers," said Rob Demain, chief executive of cybersecurity firm e2e-assure.Matt Saunders, field chief technology officer at tech consultancy Adaptavist, said it would be challenging to mitigate against a similar problem."Classic IT disaster planning strategies suggest using a second service for resilience, but in practice, it's almost impossible for a business to function without tools such as Microsoft," he said."In the wake of this outage, organisations must have a plan in place for how to work without such tools, for when incidents like this occur."

schema.headline: Microsoft 'deeply sorry' for global outage after almost 24 hours of disruption

title: Rosalía scoops historic third best album award at Latin Grammys
description: Image source, EPAImage caption, Rosalía released her fourth album Lux last year to rave reviews ByRiyah CollinsBBC NewsbeatUpdated 11:38 GMTSpanish st
body: Image source, EPAImage caption, Rosalía released her fourth album Lux last year to rave reviews ByRiyah CollinsBBC NewsbeatUpdated 11:38 GMTSpanish star Rosalía has made history as the first woman to win the best album award at the Latin Grammys three times, after being recognised for her project Lux. The singer took home five trophies in total, including two for her track La Perla which was named song of the year and best pop song.La Perla was also nominated for record of the year but missed out to Argentine singer Milo J's song Niño.Rosalía released Lux last year to rave reviews and collecting her award at the ceremony in Las Vegas on Thursday, she said: "To all the people who told me I wasn't good enough, or that my music was too weird, I'm thankful I didn't listen."The Barcelona-born artist then added: "Now I'm winning these prizes."Rosalía, who opened the ceremony with a performance of some of her biggest songs, was honoured with the prize for best alternative music album.She also picked up best shortform music video for her track Sauvignon Blanc. The singer had previously won best album for El Mal Querer in 2019 and Motomami in 2022 - and her third Lux is also tipped to be a favourite when nominations are announced for the Grammys next week.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, After a career spanning three decades, Daddy Yankee was recognised with a lifetime achievement awardIt was also a big night for Puerto Rican reggaeton legend Daddy Yankee, who won the person of the year award.He performed some of his best-loved tracks including Gasolina and Con Calma, and was joined on stage by rappers including LL Cool J and French Montana.Punjabi singer Diljit Dosanjh, who collabed with Daddy Yankee on Pokito, even took a break from his Aura India tour for the set, making him the first Indian artist to perform at the Latin Grammys.Dosanjh superfan Devanshi Arora described the singer's appearance as "a cultural revolution"."It's really invigorating and motivating to see someone from my country has made it all around the world," she tells Newsbeat.She sees a lot of similarities between South American and Punjabi communities and hopes this leads to more collaborations - with a link-up between Dosanjh and Bad Bunny top of her wishlist.Daddy Yankee was presented with the lifetime achievement award by Janet Jackson, who told him in Spanish that his music "has inspired an entire generation".Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Diljit Dosanjh became the first Indian artist to perform at the Latin GrammysAccepting the prize for record of the year, Milo J seemed surprised to have won ahead of strong competition from Karol G, Jorge Drexler, Carin León as well as Rosalía.The 20-year-old took home four trophies in the end and gave a shout out to Argentine folk music.He described Niño as the song "I'm most proud of out of everything I've created so far"."Long live Argentine folk music," he added.Elsewhere, ARIA VEGA was named best new artist and songwriter of the year went to Sara Schell.Additional reporting by Abu Bakar YasinListen to Newsbeat live at 12:45 and 17:45 weekdays - or listen back here.

schema.headline: Rosalía scoops historic third best album award at Latin Grammys

title: Before Scott Colom, these two men were the last black US senators from Mississippi
description: Figure caption, Why Democrat Scott Colom’s win in Mississippi Senate race is so significantByAlex BoydAfter winning a close race in Mississippi, Democ
body: Figure caption, Why Democrat Scott Colom’s win in Mississippi Senate race is so significantByAlex BoydAfter winning a close race in Mississippi, Democrat Scott Colom will become the state's first black US senator for more than 150 years, and the third in history.It is a historic result in the deeply conservative southern state that last sent a Democrat to the US Senate in 1982, and had not seated a black senator since 1875.Colom follows Hiram Revels, who became the first black person ever to serve in the chamber when he was seated from 1870 to 1871, and Blanche Bruce, whose term ran from 1875 to 1881. Revels and Bruce were both members of the Republican Party.Revels was chosen as Mississippi's first senator after the Civil War, serving for just over a year and campaigning strongly for racial equality.A few years later, Bruce, who was born into slavery, became the first black person to serve a full term in the US Senate. He remained in Washington after leaving the chamber and held a role in the Treasury.Both terms came before the repressive Jim Crow laws began to enforce racial segregation across Mississippi and other southern US states.Image source, Smith Collection / Archive Photos via Getty ImagesImage caption, Blanche Bruce (L) and Hiram Revels (R) are the two previous black senators to have been chosen by MississippiA significant factor in Colom's victory was his success in mobilising young people and the state's large black population, who are expected to have turned out in high numbers.In a victory speech, Colom referenced how Revels, who was a minister and served as a chaplain during the Civil War, gained support for his Senate campaign through his words."That's an example of the power of prayer, and through our history, there are so many people that lifted this state up through the power of prayer in very dark times," Colom said.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, A portrait of Hiram Revels, taken in about 1870Prior to the result being called, the BBC spoke to students at Jackson State University, a historically black college in Mississippi. Many of them had voted for the first time and backed Colom."I really feel like a change is what we need," 18-year-old Jamyria Dunn said."I've had some amazing days in my life," she continued, "but seeing Mississippi, this state in particular, turn blue, would really bring a light to my heart that people just would not understand."

schema.headline: Before Scott Colom, these two men were the last black US senators from Mississippi

title: Bessent blames Lutnick's department for Nvidia chip sales to Megaspeed
description: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has blamed Howard Lutnick's Commerce Department for failing to properly oversee the export of high-spec AI chips,
body: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has blamed Howard Lutnick's Commerce Department for failing to properly oversee the export of high-spec AI chips, as the fallout from the Nvidia scandal widens to President Donald Trump's cabinet.Pressure is building on Lutnick from across the political spectrum to explain his department's actions. Jensen Huang was ousted as Nvidia CEO after revelations he had an affair with a businesswoman who was also allegedly a Chinese spy. Megaspeed, the firm she worked for, had been probed by US government agencies over suspicions it was smuggling Nvidia chips into China, reports said, but it is not on a list of firms US companies are prevented from working with.Bessent told CNBC several agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months"."But Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process," he added.Bessent's comments come after Lutnick was called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over the Commerce Department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips.Other congressional committees have asked both Lutnick and his department to retain all records relating to Nvidia and Huang.Bessent said he was "frustrated" by delays in putting the company on the export control list and reports of leakage of AI chips into China."President Trump made it very clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above H100s, so any leakage is very frustrating because it hurts our great companies in the AI race, because it gives the Chinese an advantage," he said.Last year, the Commerce Department had been investigating Megaspeed over suspicions it had been smuggling some of Nvidia's advanced AI chips into China, according to the New York Times. Megaspeed has been contacted for comment.There was also pressure on the Commerce Department to add it to the list, but separate reporting in the Financial Times said the department was delaying efforts to have the cloud computing firm included. However, Bessent also pointed the finger at Nvidia."The story has been thus far of Jensen Huang's personal foibles," he told CNBC's Squawk Box programme, external."The real story here should be: Did Nvidia know their client, and was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies?"It's important that anyone at the company there be held accountable for that."Bessent's pointed comments are a rare instance of internal debate within the Trump administration spilling out into the public view, although tensions have reportedly simmered between Bessent and Lutnick in the past. In 2024, the two reportedly jostled for the role of treasury secretary ahead of Trump's return to the White House, and last year the pair butted heads over the administration's tariff policy, accoprding to US media. Huang has been summoned to testify before the Senate Banking Committee about his alleged affair with the former Megaspeed executive, who is suspected of being a Chinese spy.The commerce secretary has also been summoned to appear before the committee in December."Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive US technology," committee chairman, Republican Senator Tim Scott posted on X.Democrats on key congressional committees have asked the Commerce Department and Lutnick to keep all records relating to decisions to allow Nvidia to sell its advanced AI chips to Chinese companies, including all their communications with or about Nvidia and Jensen Huang.Ways and Means Committee Ranking Member Richard E Neal and Senate Finance Committee Ranking Member Ron Wyden are starting investigations into the way Nvidia was allowed to sell these chips.According to Neal and Wyden, Nvidia's advanced H200 chips could be sold to Chinese firms if they were first imported from their manufacturing facility in Taiwan into America for inspection.A 25% tariff - a levy that is paid to the federal government - was imposed on those chips, under a section of the Trade Act that Neal and Wyden say is meant to allow the US president to take action against imports that risk national security."Trump's use of the statute appears to have done the opposite, undermining US national security and putting Americans at risk," they said.

schema.headline: Bessent blames Lutnick's department for Nvidia chip sales to Megaspeed

title: Why midterm vote-counting is taking so long in Alaska Senate race
description: For the last few weeks, in addition to its usual payload of passengers, medicine, and supplies, Alaska Seaplanes has carried some unique cargo: ballot
body: For the last few weeks, in addition to its usual payload of passengers, medicine, and supplies, Alaska Seaplanes has carried some unique cargo: ballots.The regional airline is a piece of a complex logistical puzzle that sees Alaskans' midterms elections votes cast by mail and in person carried across the vast expanse of America's largest state, which is primarily connected by water and air rather than roads. This considerable task explains why, a week after most US states knew their results in the midterms - in which the Democrats won back both chambers of Congress from the Republicans - Alaskans are still waiting for the Senate race to be called. The victor in this close contest between the incumbent Republican Dan Sullivan and his Democratic challenger, former congresswoman Mary Peltola, could remain  unknown until 18 November, when officials expect to have counted all eligible ballots. "We do feel a sense of pride of making sure we do the job right - the really complicated job of getting all these ballots across thousands of miles in Alaska," Andy Kline, the marketing director of Alaska Seaplanes, which serves the south-eastern part of the state, told the BBC. "We feel like we're part of the last leg of that journey of those ballots."Some precincts in Alaska are able to communicate their initial results to centralised election offices on election night, allowing state officials and news outlets to report some preliminary vote tallies. But it takes time for the full picture of how people have voted to emerge.As well as having the logistical challenge of counting votes from across a state more than six times the size of the UK, there is a delay waiting for mail ballots to arrive, says Charles Stewart, an election expert at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. These are allowed to arrive up to 10 days later, or 15 days for overseas voters, if postmarked by election day.Stewart said that election officials had "chosen to err on the side of getting it right rather than a rush to report the second and third tranches of ballots that get counted".Regardless of whether ballots were cast in person or by mail, all of them eventually wind up in the state capital of Juneau – which is only reachable by plane or boat – for scanning and counting.While more urban districts can get their materials on a plane late on election night, it takes longer for smaller or more remote parts of Alaska.In some places, "you get someone who's basically running the election for their family and their neighbours because it's such a small village", says Scott Kendall, an election lawyer who previously worked on two campaigns for Alaska's other Republican senator, Lisa Murkowski. In these smaller areas, ballots are sealed up in special envelopes or containers and sent it through the mail - which is where companies like Alaska Seaplanes comes in. Ballots are put on the planes and sent to Juneau, where they then get dropped at the post office and delivered."It's part of our daily routine, just another couple of boxes," Kline said.

schema.headline: Why midterm vote-counting is taking so long in Alaska Senate race

title: Why is Microsoft's outage lasting so long and will emails be lost?
description: Some Microsoft 365 services have been affected by "connectivity problems" with problems reported in at least 74 countries.From late on Thursday, custo
body: Some Microsoft 365 services have been affected by "connectivity problems" with problems reported in at least 74 countries.From late on Thursday, customers reported varying levels of access - many were unable to send or receive emails, view certain files or details on their calendar apps. But some users were able to use Teams, messaging and online meeting functions without issues. As of Friday afternoon, Microsoft said it had seen "encouraging recovery progress" in Europe and improvement in North America.The company added that it was focused on "addressing the remaining areas of disruption" but warned "some users may still experience intermittent issues".In a later statement, the company said it was continuing to see improvements "with email queues significantly reduced and approaching normal levels".The company attributed the ongoing outage to an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade."We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions," it said on Friday.Although email service Outlook appears to be resuming, the outage has so far lasted for more than 20 hours - in outage terms that is considered a long time.Prof James Ferryman from the University of Reading's department of computer science said the details the company has disclosed provide some clues."What Microsoft has told us is that the part of its servers that sets up secure connections is getting swamped, and once that happens the server just stops answering," he said."The trouble is that this kind of failure snowballs."One server falls over, its work gets passed to the next one, and meanwhile huge numbers of phones and laptops keep trying to get back in."You can't just turn it all back on at once. You have to bring it back bit by bit."The challenge is therefore not just fixing the fault, but managing the huge surge of devices trying to reconnect once services start coming back online.Gergely Orosz, a former leading software engineer at several major tech companies including Skype and Uber, said this could be the "most disruptive" business email outage "of all time".He said it was still difficult to know just how many people have been affected by the disruption, but added he "cannot recall" an outage over business email ever taking this long to return to normal.Australian cyber-security expert Troy Hunt told the BBC the outage could have far-reaching consequences."Microsoft is a massive part of the internet backbone and reminds us how critical email still is. "Not only does this outage affect many people's ability to work but also things like the ability to communicate about appointments, purchase things that need verification, create or access accounts and services," he said.In a statement, Microsoft said it was "deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners. "We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously. We are seeing broad recovery and stability across our services."More than 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps according to Microsoft's website. The full scale of the outage has not been confirmed.Microsoft 365 is used by companies worldwide and is expected to have a knock-on effect to other services.Tech giants OpenAI and Anthropic both earlier reported problems as a result of the outage.ChatGPT-maker OpenAI said it was investigating an issue affecting its connections to Microsoft's services, which had caused some tools to not work as expected.From city governments in the US to Australian spy agencies, disruption across the globe has been widespread.Courts from Los Angeles to Texas earlier warned that communications might be delayed.In Canada, the public broadcaster CBC reported that a healthcare network running several hospitals in Toronto was experiencing email issues, but that patient care was not affected.The government of Japan also said its shared IT platform had been disrupted.Across the UK, GP surgeries, pharmacies, police and schools have been affected by the outage.Some GP surgeries had urged patients not to submit messages via their website while police forces were also earlier asking the public to call if they want to make a report.Additional reporting by Henry Moore

schema.headline: Why is Microsoft's outage lasting so long and will emails be lost?

title: Pat Cummins: Australian cricket's sandpapergate is back, reopening wounds in a 'nation of good sports'
description: As Australian cricket captain Pat Cummins spent more than an hour being grilled by reporters over one of sport's biggest cheating scandals, the tensio
body: As Australian cricket captain Pat Cummins spent more than an hour being grilled by reporters over one of sport's biggest cheating scandals, the tension in the hall was occasionally pierced by muffled cheers.Outside, a crucial match in the top tier of domestic cricket was getting under way. Cummins was clear he'd rather we all be talking about that.But inside the nets at Cricket Central in Sydney, he faced more than a dozen TV cameras and a gaggle of journalists several times as large. His goal: to put rumours of his involvement in "sandpapergate" to rest."I don't want to talk about this again after today," he said. "Even if it takes all day... I'll stay here until we have no more questions."A book by his friend and former teammate Usman Khawaja has renewed scrutiny on a 2018 plot to tamper with the ball using sandpaper in Australia's third Test match against South Africa in Cape Town. Three players admitted they were involved at the time and were handed lengthy bans, but in a memoir released last week, Khawaja said the entire Australian team knew about the sandpaper scheme.His claims have plunged the Australian cricket world into chaos, thrown speculation over key figures from that Test - including star bowler Cummins who has since risen to hold what many joke is Australia's most important job - and reopened wounds for fans.Josh, 28, told the BBC he thought everyone had moved on: "It's just a bit crazy that it's all blown up again... I think it is a bit ridiculous, after eight years.""I'm a bit bored of it," another spectator at the New South Wales vs South Australia Sheffield Shield match said.Among fans, there's frustration that Khawaja has chosen to come forward now, almost a decade on and at the start of an exciting summer, and year, of cricket. Though there's an argument there'd never be a good time for Khawaja, who retired from international cricket in January, to make these allegations. There's worry about the impact on the men's team's performance this summer, after a lacklustre showing in South Africa last month - its first Test matches there since the 2018 incident.And there's a sense of injustice that Australia can't seem to escape the scandal, given - according to many players themselves - how common boundary-bending on ball tampering apparently was in that era."It's a bit of a stitch up," 21-year-old James said."Every country has done it... if it wasn't us, it was probably going to be someone else."Khawaja's memoir is also causing rancour among current and former players and coaches.In it, he said he had wanted the team to take collective responsibility for the tampering after batsman Cameron Bancroft was caught with the sandpaper on field."I said: 'Take this as a team. We did this as a team. We knew what was going on, and we have to take it as a team'."However Khawaja has since said he didn't want to start a "witch hunt" and has refused to answer questions on exactly who he claims knew of the scheme, and what they knew.David Warner, who received the most severe punishment of the Cape Town trio, said Khawaja had written the truth and that Cummins' press conference denying the claims "threw him under the bus".Steve Smith, the captain at the time who was also suspended, has been travelling overseas and is yet to say anything publicly about the claims in the book. Bancroft is also staying silent for now despite previously suggesting the bowlers knew.But half of Australia's living cricket royalty and a slew of former coaches - some of whom have been accused of wrongdoing too - have thrown in their two cents.And Cricket Australia is under pressure from some to reopen its investigation into sandpapergate - something chief executive Todd Greenberg has already ruled out.Prof David Rowe of the University of Western Sydney told the BBC the saga was still so painful for many players and fans as the country sees itself as "a nation of good sports"."The idea of being a good sport is two things. One is being good at sport, so you actually win. But the other side is that you do it honourably and fairly," he said."Many Australians would see themselves as above all that. That is: cheating is what other teams get up to... not the nation of good sports."He said the revelation was a "nasty shock" which brought the country "collective shame" which lingers today.He says he doubts that the cricket scene would be able to move on without a fresh response from the governing body, Cricket Australia."One of the best ways to fuel conspiracy theories and keep sandpapergate going is to essentially say 'there's no more to see here' - especially when that comes from the authorities," Rowe said.Asked about a fresh investigation, Cummins said it was a matter for Cricket Australia.Over the marathon press conference - which one reporter suggested was the longest in Australian sporting history - Cummins was cautious, pausing often to consider his responses and to make sure they answered the questions being asked of him.But he was also frank - using strong words to reject what he said were "vague" claims by Khawaja and admitting he was frustrated a friend had put him in this position. "Friends aren't casual with each other's lives and reputations... That's something I've been grappling with the last couple of days."As the reporters ran out of steam, Cummins said it was "annoying" that sandpapergate scandal was still a distraction for Australian cricket. He gestured outside to the Sheffield Shield match and mentioned Friday's one-day international against England in Perth, from which he and other key players are being rested."It's been eight years... Hopefully today we put a line through it and we're done and we can all move on to much more fun topics, like actual cricket."Few people think he'll get his wish."It's going to be hard to move on, given that there's two sides of the story and it doesn't look like either side is going to back down," James said."I don't know what the outcome will be."

schema.headline: Pat Cummins: Australian cricket's sandpapergate is back, reopening wounds in a 'nation of good sports'

title: Ethiopia's Tigray conflict: Has Abiy Ahmed defeated the TPLF?
description: Running a hair salon in Mekelle, capital of Ethiopia's troubled northern Tigray region, is not easy at the moment."People can't prioritise beauty over
body: Running a hair salon in Mekelle, capital of Ethiopia's troubled northern Tigray region, is not easy at the moment."People can't prioritise beauty over daily basic needs. For many residents, thinking about self-care is a luxury, at a time when they can't feed their kids," Firut Me'ar, who runs a salon in the city, tells the BBC.After a brief war, the city is under the control of the national army but life is far from normal, says Firut, a single mother of a 10-year-old daughter."Things are better than during the war, but people still have no money, no morale. Business is almost non-existent," she says, her voice shaking with emotion.Above all, she says people are worried about what the future holds. "There is uncertainty about what comes next."Fighting broke out in late September between the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the party that had run Tigray for decades, and the national army - a resumption of the two-year civil war that officially ended in 2022.But within less than two weeks, federal forces marched triumphantly into Mekelle. The TPLF made what it called a "strategic withdrawal" from the city and Tigray's other main towns so the army encountered little resistance. Hundreds of people are reported to have died in the conflict, including dozens killed by drone strikes and bombing raids by the air force.Ethiopian government officials and supporters argue that the war is effectively over and that the only remaining task is to clear Tigray of TPLF elements.Getachew Reda, a senior TPLF official who switched sides and is now an adviser to the prime minister, declared that the war in Tigray had ended and that stabilising the region should now be the immediate priority.Cameroon Hudson, an analyst and consultant on African peace and security, says there are various reasons for the TPLF's rapid defeat."The TPLF has lost popular support at home. It is fragmented, it does not possess the advanced military technology necessary to match the ENDF [Ethiopian National Defence Forces]," he says. "It has lost many of its generals, strategic thinkers, finest diplomats and fighters, either through defections or arrests. The infighting within the TPLF leadership has caused significant damage."Abraha Hailezgi, a scholar at Mekelle University, agrees. "The army lacks a clear political vision. In recent years, it has become associated with coercion, abuses, forced recruitment and arbitrary actions. As a result, many people have come to view the TPLF army as an adversary rather than a force acting on their behalf," he says.Speaking by telephone from an undisclosed location, TPLF spokesperson Mikael Asgedom denies that the group has lost.Instead, he describes it as a deliberate tactical and strategic retreat. "This is not a defeat," he tells the BBC.He says the TPLF "intentionally allowed the ENDF to advance deeper into the heartland of Tigray", where it can be isolated and confronted on favourable terrain. "We chose not to fight on terms favourable to the enemy."The TPLF is preparing for a major counteroffensive, he says, adding that TPLF fighters have launched attacks against Ethiopian forces in several locations following their withdrawal from the region's towns, arguing that these operations demonstrated the group's continued military capability.It is hard to get verified information from Tigray and the BBC is unable to report from there. But phone lines and the internet, which were cut when fighting broke out, have now been restored.Residents in different parts of Tigray tell the BBC that fighting is continuing in central, northern and north-western parts of Tigray, with the use of heavy artillery and drone strikes.Eyewitnesses around Sheraro, a town near the Eritrean border, report heavy fighting involving artillery and ground forces in recent days."We could hear heavy artillery fire from the Sheraro direction. People are concerned because there is no sense of security," a businessman tells the BBC on condition of anonymity. He adds that military convoys from both sides had moved towards Sheraro, while a motorcycle operator in the southern town of Yechila says military checkpoints are still active.Memories of the devastating 2020-2022 Tigray war remain raw for many residents. The conflict saw widespread human rights abuses and allegations of ethnic cleansing in Western Tigray, while estimates suggest the war claimed hundreds of thousands of lives. As soldiers from Eritrea, accused of some of the worst atrocities in the previous conflict, and Ethiopia have reappeared in Tigray's towns, many residents describe a profound sense of fear and anxiety, saying the sight of the troops has reopened still-fresh wounds.Military sources aligned with the federal army say operations against the TPLF are continuing, with recent fighting and troop movements reported in northern Tigray, near the Eritrean border, as well as across central Tigray's rugged highlands. They claim the TPLF's capabilities are being steadily degraded.Security analysts and observers agree that unrest is likely to continue for some time. "I see a situation in which there could be a prolonged war in Tigray," Yared Tibebu, a well-known Ethiopian commentator based in the US, tells the BBC.Yared argues that the TPLF has a long history of waging protracted armed struggles and believes the movement is once again preparing for a lengthy conflict. He believes that once the group has reorganised its military and political structures, it may attempt to resume offensive operations. However he believes this will not happen for some time because of internal divisions - a suggestion dismissed by TPLF spokesperson Mikael.Hudson rejects the idea that Tigray is heading towards a prolonged war but agrees that the region may not be truly peaceful for some time. "The TPLF may continue a low-level insurgency and guerrilla campaign, but that is not war. I do not think there will be a wider-scale conflict between the federal forces and the TPLF."He says the TPLF no longer possesses the size, strength or military capability required to effectively confront federal forces, which he says have significantly expanded and modernised in recent years. "The TPLF has also lost much of its public support and cannot easily rebuild its ranks through recruitment," he says.Yared, on the other hand, points to the TPLF's history of overcoming setbacks as evidence that the movement could recover to sustain a prolonged struggle. "The TPLF has overcome many major challenges in the past. It is wrong to conclude that it has no public support. It is a political movement with a history stretching back more than 50 years," he says.What Yared sees as a strength, Hudson sees as a weakness, saying the TPLF is still "trapped in the past", and continues to behave as a dominant party within Tigray, even though the situation has changed. "It is a movement that has not evolved, modernised or expanded."While Hudson argues that the TPLF is not equipped to sustain a major military campaign, the TPLF spokesman says the group obtains weapons and logistical supplies from the Ethiopian military. "We seize weapons from our enemy, and the weaponry that has entered Tigray will, sooner or later, become ours."In early October, eyewitnesses told the BBC they had seen Eritrean troops in Tigray amid reports they were backing the TPLF.  However, they appear to have returned home and Hudson thinks the country would be wary of becoming further embroiled in the conflict."First, Eritrea does not have unlimited resources. Second, the TPLF is no more an effective military force, and Eritrean leaders may have concluded that supporting it at this stage would not yield significant military gains," he says. "Third, Eritrea would have to consider the risk of provoking a confrontation with Ethiopia if it openly backs the TPLF."Sources in the Ethiopia army tell the BBC that senior members of the TPLF's political leadership were briefly based in Eritrea, however, they say the authorities ordered them to leave in early November, shortly after President Isaias Afwerki returned from Russia. According to the sources, the move was driven by concerns that Ethiopia could use their presence as a reason to invade.Hudson also argues that Eritrea's renewed diplomatic engagement with the US, whose relations with the TPLF have long been strained, could further discourage Asmara from providing meaningful support to the movement.In September, seven Ethiopian rebel groups led by the TPLF announced the formation of a new coalition called the Alliance for Survival, aimed at removing Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government.Yared believes the alliance could give the TPLF the strength to keep on fighting. "Its members can combine their strengths. The TDF [the TPLF's military wing] has leadership experience and organisational capacity, while Fano [an ethnic Amhara militia] is believed to have between 70,000 and 80,000 fighters."If conditions emerge that allow the forces to co-ordinate effectively, the TPLF's current difficulties may not last long," he says.Hudson, however, rejects that argument, insisting that the alliance is unlikely to alter the balance of power. "I don't think the TPLF can be saved by this alliance. The ethnic militias have not demonstrated the capacity, either individually or collectively, to pose a serious threat to federal forces. We should not underestimate the strength of the federal army," he says.Abraha from Mekelle University argues that the conflict in Tigray will only truly be over if the federal government addresses the region's feeling that it has been marginalised, both economically and politically by the current government. However, many Tigrayan elites and political observers remain wary of the federal government's intentions. They question whether the authorities in Addis Ababa are genuinely seeking to address Tigray's problems, or whether they are taking advantage of the region's weakness to boost their influence.In the meantime, many ordinary people in Tigray say their priority is peace."Peace seems slow in coming. Most people are tired of politics. Whatever happens, we only want peace and a chance to rebuild our lives," says Firut from her beauty salon in Mekelle.

schema.headline: Ethiopia's Tigray conflict: Has Abiy Ahmed defeated the TPLF?

title: Formula 1's diamond 'heist': an unsolved mystery?
description: Where were you between the hours of 1pm and 3pm on 23 May 2004?If you were in Monaco, consider yourself a suspect - or at least a witness - in Formula
body: Where were you between the hours of 1pm and 3pm on 23 May 2004?If you were in Monaco, consider yourself a suspect - or at least a witness - in Formula 1's biggest unsolved mystery.A $300,000 diamond was last seen stuck to the front of an F1 car before it crashed on the first lap of the Grand Prix and it still has not been found 22 years later.Did someone pick it up? Was it swept up with all the debris? Did it slip down a drain? Was it even a real diamond?Someone, somewhere, knows something.The reason why a 1.4 carat diamond was attached to the most delicate part of a car that reaches 200mph in a race was straightforward: publicity.Jaguar Racing's results on the track had been mediocre at best since becoming an F1 team in 2000 and by 2004 its parent company Ford had decided it would be pulling them out of the sport."My job flipped from primarily running the team to primarily selling the team and finding a new owner or they would shut it down," former team principal Tony Purnell tells BBC Sport."It was probably the worst year of my life. Particularly because for the first few months I was sworn to secrecy."His team needed some good PR to divert attention away from performance and improve its appeal.They had enjoyed a successful promotional weekend in Silverstone the previous season thanks to a tie-up with Terminator 3 and so director of communications Nav Sidhu was looking to recreate the magic with another bit of help from a movie."I'd heard on the grapevine, around about the winter of 2003, that they were making Ocean's Twelve and we discovered that they were shooting some of the scenes in Monte Carlo," Sidhu says."One thing led to another and before you knew it, we had agreed [a deal] with George Clooney, Brad Pitt and Matt Damon."Sidhu had arranged with legendary Hollywood producer Jerry Weintraub to have the film's branding and stars take over the team for the Monaco weekend.The film plot centred on an audacious theft of a diamond-encrusted Faberge egg. Sidhu decided he wanted some sparkle on his cars too at the most glamorous race in the F1 calendar.Sidhu negotiated with diamond company Steinmetz that the two Jaguar cars would have gems - which would today be worth about $1m in total - attached to them.What happened next, though, was not part of the script.While the champagne corks were popping on nearby mega yachts in the principality, the diamonds were being hand-delivered into the garages. There were two that would be mounted on to the car and a larger gem just for the photos.The diamonds for the cars were encased by steel and fixed to the nose cones. One on experienced driver Mark Webber's car and one on rookie Christian Klien's.Webber was starting from 11th place in the grid and Klien - in only his sixth race - was starting from 14th. They weren't expected to challenge for the podium, but they were expected to bring the diamonds back.Monaco's street circuit is demanding, with narrow roads, tight turns and a tunnel.Overtaking is difficult and crashes are common - as Klien soon found out.In a chaotic first lap, the Austrian made contact with one of the Jordan cars exiting the Mirabeau corner. This damaged the front of his car - where the diamond was - and led to a slow collision with the barriers at the famous Loews hairpin.Klien climbed out unhurt but the front of the car was crumpled.It was not long before Sidhu had the diamond company on the phone asking if they would get their diamond back."I can't remember what I answered, but it certainly wasn't 'yes'," he says.He couldn't even get on to the track to have a look as the race had another 76 laps to go and only then would the car - which had been lifted off the track by a crane and left behind the barriers - return to the garage."I was consumed with getting to that spot as quickly as I possibly could," Sidhu says."That hour and a half waiting for the race to finish felt like a day and a half, every single lap was just like pulling teeth."By the time he had the chance to have a look, there was no sign of the diamond.But there were plenty of theories.Theory: it was not a real diamondSidhu completely denies the rumours of a fake diamond."I've learned that any diamond company is not going to go out there, particularly in the public domain, and use fake diamonds because clearly there's a high risk of being caught," he says."Had we used a fake diamond in that car and what took place took place, then clearly the embarrassment and the disrepute it would bring Jaguar, and Formula 1 for that matter, was too high risk."There's been loads of conspiracy theories about was it a real diamond or was Christian told to crash his car and I think that's what's given the story its life - there's a mystery to this story and that mystery will always breed different theories."Purnell backs up the legitimacy of the diamond, recalling a conversation he had with the managing director of the team, David Pitchforth."David said, 'Tony, it was definitely real because when they came to the office with it, I picked the diamond up, went to the window and scratched the window' because that's how to tell."Hearing that from Dave, I'm in no doubt it was the real thing that was put on the car."I don't know if one of our mechanics was switched on enough to make a fake, but I don't think so."Theory: someone pocketed it"I think somebody probably just picked it up, put it in their pocket and... they're probably smiling and thinking, 'it's in my drawer'," says Purnell."I do think also that a fairly large diamond zooming through at 100 miles an hour probably shattered. Somebody's got a little bit, somebody else has got another [little bit]."Maybe, sadly, just some guy was sweeping up the road or one of those trucks with the brushes and it all went down the sewer."It did occur to me that the ultimate thing would be if Clooney, Pitt and Damon had contrived to steal it because it was so in line with Ocean's Eleven. But that was a fantasy too far."There would have been hundreds, if not thousands, of people in the area because within an hour or so of the end of the race the circuit would have been returned to public roads.   Sidhu is pretty certain about what happened to the diamond: "Someone's picked it up."What people tend to do is, believe it or not, pick up bits of tyre rubber, you know, claim that as Michael Schumacher's front tyre rubber or whatever they can find."Somebody may have picked it up not having any idea it came off a car."There's a lot of diamonds in Monte Carlo. There's a lot of people walking around Monte Carlo with a lot of jewellery and a lot of stones."Somebody dropped a diamond in Monte Carlo. Well, they're not going to miss that, are they? Probably not."Theory: Klien crashed on purposeSidhu says the cost of the damage to the car was more than the cost of the diamond, which reports at the time said was uninsured.And points and a good result in the race were more valuable to the team and individuals than a diamond or the publicity a crash would bring. It was simply not worth crashing on purpose."For us, bringing two cars home, ideally in the points, had far bigger commercial benefits to us in terms of constructors' points, broadcast money, and more importantly, trying to retain our sponsors and trying to protect the integrity of the team," Sidhu explains.Klien drove straight into the barriers right in front of the marshals so would not have had the chance to start looking for a diamond or picking it up even if he had wanted to."Christian didn't try and say all the brakes failed or anything like that, he's just said 'I made a rookie mistake'," says Purnell."He was a young guy, first time, made a mistake, it happens. Doesn't usually happen with a $300,000 diamond flying into the crowd or wherever it went, but I'm sure Christian wasn't really aware of the diamond."No amount of money would have got Christian to do that [crash on purpose]. He wanted to make a success of what he was doing."While events were unfolding, Purnell had not really been thinking about the diamond. His main concern that day was that one of his drivers had crashed and the other also did not finish, and that this was not a good look in terms of pleasing current backers or attracting potential buyers."When Christian went into the wall and then later Mark retired, my entire thinking was 'Oh God. What am I going to say?' The chairman of HSBC [Jaguar's then sponsors] was there, Sir John Bond. Jackie [Stewart] was there."It was all about 'how am I going to explain another bad performance? How am I going to say 'just stick with the plan? We know what we're doing, it will take time' because sponsors don't have time. They want success."In the end, the missing diamond came to the rescue."No-one mentioned Jarno Trulli winning the Grand Prix, no-one asked how the Jaguars did. No-one was interested that Mark Webber's car broke as well. It was, 'where's the diamond?'" says Purnell."I remember talking to somebody in Detroit saying, 'fantastic publicity over here, you know we never hear anything about Formula 1 but it's on the newscasts, it's in the papers - fantastic'."Asked if the diamond mystery had helped the eventual sale of the team to Red Bull six months later, he replies: "I think that helped quite a lot because it buzzed the Jaguar team and showed that huge publicity was possible even if you weren't doing so well."Red Bull went on to become hugely successful, winning eight drivers' championships and six constructors' championships since joining F1."You couldn't design a better PR weekend," says Purnell.Even if it was not quite how it was planned and there is still the small matter of a missing diamond.

title: At least 24 killed after bus collides with truck near Kaziranga National Park
description: The bus was carrying passengers from Bokakhat and was headed towards Nagaon. Bokakhat is best known as the gateway to Kaziranga National Park, famous
body: The bus was carrying passengers from Bokakhat and was headed towards Nagaon. Bokakhat is best known as the gateway to Kaziranga National Park, famous for its one-horned rhinoceroses.Nagaon is an important agricultural and commercial centre in central Assam, about 120km (74.5 miles) west of Bokakhat by road.Lurinjyoti Gogoi, chief of a regional opposition party, said road safety has long been a major concern in the state."The government must take it up seriously," he said.Road accidents are responsible for thousands of deaths in India every year.In 2023, 172,000 people lost their lives on Indian roads, or 474 a day – roughly one every three minutes.The count increased to 183,382 deaths in 2025.Experts say the crisis is rooted not just in infrastructure but in human behaviour, enforcement gaps and systemic neglect.

schema.headline: At least 24 killed after bus collides with truck near Kaziranga National Park

title: German spies handed new powers to tackle 'hybrid threats' from abroad
description: Germany's foreign and domestic intelligence services are to be given greater powers to combat espionage, terrorism and sabotage after the country's pa
body: Germany's foreign and domestic intelligence services are to be given greater powers to combat espionage, terrorism and sabotage after the country's parliament, the Bundestag, approved a major overhaul of its legislation.Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, who championed the bill, has called it a "reform of the century", necessary because of the increasing threats from foreign powers.But the Left Party's security spokeswoman, Clara Bünger, said Dobrindt was creating a new German secret police.The legislation gives numerous new powers to Germany's BND federal intelligence service, and its BfV domestic service, the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution.In the Bundestag, 309 MPs voted in favour of the new law on intelligence services, while 190 voted against and 71 abstained.For historical reasons, German intelligence has mainly focused on gathering information rather than acting on it. In future, German spies working for the BND, which is responsible for foreign intelligence, will be able to conduct covert operations abroad, including sabotage.This could include paralysing the servers of state-sponsored hacker groups, disrupting disinformation networks, or even disrupting supply chains for weapons.Agents for the domestic intelligence service, the BfV, will no longer to be limited to gathering information. For the first time they will be able to take protective action against property and IT systems, if specific threats are identified.That means they will be allowed to dismantle or break explosives or weapons, divert or block data flows during cyber-attacks, delete or falsify data stored for malicious purposes, and plant false information on those involved.Under certain conditions, BfV agents will also be permitted to enter homes covertly. However, the measure must always be authorised in advance.They will also be given wider powers of digital surveillance, including monitoring encrypted telecommunications and carrying out online searches. They will also be allowed to use AI-supported data analysis and biometric image matching on the internet.The government says the reform is needed because of an increase in foreign espionage, particularly from Russia, China and Iran."We are the target of hybrid threats," said Dobrindt. "Germany is a theatre of operations for terrorism, extremism and foreign powers."In August, a drone carrying an explosive device was discovered at Leipzig Airport, close to Ukrainian cargo planes. However, it failed to explode as the bomb's detonator was apparently faulty.German authorities say Russia was behind the attack.The new law has been bitterly criticised by some opposition politicians, even though Dobrindt has said it is "madness" to think it means that Germany is creating a new secret police.And Clara Bünger from the Left Party told public broadcaster ARD that the new law was "a monster… summoning ghosts that we will probably never be able to get rid of".The separation between the police and the secret service, she warned, was "being eroded" - and Bünger said that had been a lesson learned from the Nazi era."This means the secret service is being granted executive powers and will not only be allowed to act pre-emptively, but will also be granted police powers."However, Sonja Eichwede of the centre-left SPD, which is part of Germany's governing coalition, said the reforms would make a significant contribution to ensuring the country's democracy was "robust and resilient".

schema.headline: German spies handed new powers to tackle 'hybrid threats' from abroad
